Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette:
Dmitri Hale is a 46-year-old graphic designer of Eastern European descent who lives with his wife in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant deterioration in his functioning over the past eighteen months, and he arrived at the intake appointment visibly tense, choosing a seat near the door and glancing at it more than once before the session began.

Approximately nineteen months ago, Dmitri was walking home from a late evening at a client's studio when he witnessed a confrontation between police officers and a young man on the sidewalk outside a convenience store. What began as a stop escalated rapidly. Dmitri was close enough to see the young man's face when he was forced to the ground, close enough to hear the sounds, and close enough to see the injuries that resulted - the torn skin at the man's temple, the blood spreading against the concrete. He stood frozen for what he estimates was several minutes, unable to move or speak, before an officer turned and told him sharply to keep walking. He did. He has not been able to fully account for what happened in those minutes since.

In the weeks that followed, Dmitri noticed that something had shifted. He would be working at his desk - adjusting a layout, reviewing colour proofs - when a thought would arrive unbidden and fully formed, not as a vague impression but as something insistent and visual. The image of the wound. The particular angle of the young man's head against the pavement. He found that if he tried to sit with these intrusions and describe them, even to himself, the thread dissolved. He would begin and then simply stop, unable to locate the sequence, unable to finish the account. He told his wife once, early on, that he couldn't explain it properly. He hasn't tried again since.

Over the following months his world contracted in ways that accumulated quietly. He began avoiding the neighbourhood where the incident occurred, then broader areas of the city where police presence was likely. When he passes a patrol car now, or sees an officer on the street, the full memory returns without transition - not as a recollection but as an event happening again in the present. The same thing occurs when he encounters images of injuries on others, even incidentally: a news photograph, a scene in a film his wife is watching in the next room. His body responds before his mind catches up - shoulders rigid, jaw clenched, a readiness that does not discharge. He is unable to relax even at home, even in the evenings when he knows, rationally, that he is safe. Before entering any space - a restaurant, a client's office, even a room in his own house he hasn't been in recently - he locates the exits. He is not always aware he is doing it until it is done.

Dmitri's work has suffered in ways that are now visible to clients. He misses deadlines he would previously have met without difficulty. He spends hours on his phone between tasks - scrolling, playing games, cycling through websites - not because he finds pleasure in it but because keeping his mind occupied prevents it from going somewhere he cannot manage. He has declined two collaborative projects that would have required him to work on-site with other creatives, telling his wife he simply wasn't interested. He has become harder to reach socially, even for her. Friends have stopped calling as frequently. She has begun asking questions he doesn't know how to answer.

What brought Dmitri to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation of losses. He had come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that his life before that evening was simply gone - not damaged but destroyed, in a way that could not be repaired. What made this harder to carry was his conviction that what happened was profoundly unjust, that nothing had been done, that no one had been held accountable for what he saw, and that this absence of accountability was itself a wound that remained open. He is not certain therapy can change any of that. What he said, near the end of the intake, was that he hoped at minimum to feel like himself again - though he acknowledged he was no longer entirely sure what that meant.
